written.heading: Date
written.quote: The majority of scholars who hold to the Solomonic authorship of Ecclesiastes date the book in Solomon’s final years as king (c. 940 BC).

written.label: in the postexilic period
written.heading: Date
written.quote: Those who deny Solomonic authorship disagree among themselves as to when the book was written, but most date it in the postexilic period.

written.label: fifth-century BC
written.heading: Date
written.quote: A number of conservative scholars, such as Franz Delitzsch and E. J. Young, have assigned a fifth-century BC date to the book.

written.label: third-century BC
written.heading: Date
written.quote: Many others consider it a third-century BC document.

written.label: the latter half of the tenth century BC
written.heading: Date
written.quote: If Solomon was the author, it was written during the latter half of the tenth century BC.

written.label: before 586 BC
written.heading: Date
written.quote: But the contents indicate that the song must have been written and completed at some point during the Hebrew monarchy (before 586 BC).

written.label: about 700 BC
written.heading: Date
written.quote: Since many of the events recorded in chapters 1–39 took place during the ministry of Isaiah, most of these chapters were probably written by about 700 BC or shortly thereafter.

written.label: during Isaiah’s retirement years
written.heading: Date
written.quote: This means that some of the earlier chapters, along with 40–66, were probably written later, during Isaiah’s retirement years.

written.label: much later than Isaiah in connection with the Babylonian exile
written.heading: Author
written.quote: Chapters 40–66 contain many powerful passages that underscore the grandeur of the book. It is ironic, then, that many scholars attribute these chapters to a “second” or “third” Isaiah, unknown authors who wrote much later than Isaiah in connection with the Babylonian exile.

written.label: c. 627–586 BC
written.heading: Date
written.quote: Nonetheless, the book was written during Jeremiah’s ministry (c. 627–586 BC).

written.label: shortly after the fall of Jerusalem (586 BC)
written.heading: Date
written.quote: If the book of Lamentations was written by Jeremiah, the time of writing would be shortly after the fall of Jerusalem (586 BC).

written.label: too late for it to have been authored by Jeremiah
written.heading: Author
written.quote: Since Jeremiah is in the second division, it is argued that Lamentations was written too late for it to have been authored by Jeremiah.

written.label: from 592 BC
written.quote: Ezekiel’s ministry seems to have extended from 592 BC to at least the 27th year of the exile (29:17).

written.label: sixth century BC
written.heading: Date
written.quote: The conservative interpretation has usually been that the book was written in the sixth century BC.

written.label: about 165 BC
written.heading: Date
written.quote: An alternative position is that the book was written about 165 BC.

written.label: very near to the time of Israel’s fall (722 BC)
written.heading: Date
written.quote: These factors confirm that the compilation of Hosea’s messages may have taken place very near to the time of Israel’s fall (722 BC).

written.label: c. 400 BC
written.heading: Date
written.quote: Many different views of the date of Joel have been taken by those who have studied this book carefully; thus it is difficult to be dogmatic. The book may be dated to a time after the return to Jerusalem of the Jewish exiles who had been in Babylon—more precisely, to a time after Nehemiah’s work of rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem (c. 400 BC).

written.who: Some of those who favor a preexilic date for the book
written.label: the ninth century
written.heading: Date
written.quote: Some of those who favor a preexilic date for the book place it in the ninth century, in the early period of the reign of Joash when the king was too young to actually function as ruler of the land.

written.label: shortly before the death of Josiah in 609 BC
written.heading: Date
written.quote: Others place it sometime shortly before the death of Josiah in 609 BC because of the reference to the enemy coming from the north (as in Jeremiah) and because of the appeal to the people (like Jeremiah’s appeal) to return to the Lord with all their hearts (2:12).

written.label: about 760 BC
written.heading: Date, Origin, and Destination
written.quote: When all the evidence is taken into consideration, it seems reasonable to date the beginning of Amos’s prophecies at Bethel to about 760 BC, or approximately the middle of the period during which both Uzziah and Jeroboam II were on their thrones.

written.label: shortly before the fall of Jerusalem
written.heading: Background
written.quote: He probably had his vision concerning Edom (v 1) shortly before the fall of Jerusalem and the devastation of Judah by Nebuchadnezzar in 586 BC.

written.label: postexilic
written.heading: Date
written.quote: The postexilic Obadiah stands between the eighth-century BC prophets Amos and Micah, and in fact in the Greek OT Joel was placed in a different position from its place in the Hebrew Bible.

written.label: 793–753 BC
written.heading: Date
written.quote: If Jonah was the son of Amittai cited in 2 Kings 14:25, the prophecy would have to be dated in the reign of Jeroboam II of Israel (793–753 BC).

written.who: Those who understand the book to have been written by an author other than Jonah
written.label: from the period following the fall of Nineveh to well into the postexilic period
written.heading: Date
written.quote: Those who understand the book to have been written by an author other than Jonah place the writing at various times, from the period following the fall of Nineveh to well into the postexilic period.

written.label: the last part of the eighth century BC
written.heading: Date
written.quote: Some striking parallel passages between Micah and Isaiah (Mi 4:1-4; Is 2:2-4) and between Micah and Amos (Mi 6:10-11; Am 8:5-6) make it probable that Micah’s ministry was in the last part of the eighth century BC.

written.label: the middle of the seventh century
written.heading: Date
written.quote: Since the influence of Assyria in the western provinces began to decline in the latter half of the seventh century, it is best to place the writing of the book in the middle of the seventh century, subsequent to the destruction of Thebes but before the erosion of Assyrian power in Syro-Palestine.
written.prefersQuote: it is best to place the writing of the book in the middle of the seventh century

written.label: very close to the fall of Nineveh
written.heading: Date
written.quote: Some scholars prefer a date very close to the fall of Nineveh, perhaps during the time when Assyria was being invaded.

written.who: Scholars who deny the validity of biblical prophecy
written.label: subsequent to the fall of Nineveh
written.heading: Date
written.quote: Scholars who deny the validity of biblical prophecy generally date the book in the period subsequent to the fall of Nineveh.

written.label: between 612 and 605 BC
written.heading: Date
written.quote: Because it is also possible that he was referring to the world at large, it seems best to date Habakkuk’s ministry as starting between 612 and 605 BC, and continuing during the reign of Jehoiakim (609–598 BC).
written.prefersQuote: it seems best to date Habakkuk’s ministry as starting between 612 and 605 BC

written.label: within the reign of Josiah (640–609 BC)
written.heading: Date
written.quote: Because the Chaldeans came to power about 625 BC, many scholars think that the prophecy of Habakkuk was written shortly before that time. The book would have been written, then, within the reign of Josiah (640–609 BC).

written.label: around 630 BC
written.heading: Date, Origin, and Destination
written.quote: Zephaniah probably prophesied around 630 BC.

written.label: 520 BC
written.heading: Author and Date
written.quote: Haggai was among the Jewish colonists at Jerusalem in the year 520 BC when his prophetic words were recorded (Ezr 5:1-2; 6:14).

written.label: from 520 to 518 BC
written.heading: Background
written.quote: The first eight chapters of Zechariah are set against the social, political, and religious situations in Jerusalem from 520 to 518 BC.

written.heading: Date
written.quote: Any attempt to assign specific dates to Zechariah 9–14 would be speculation.

written.label: just after 433 BC
written.heading: Date
written.quote: The reference to “the governor” in Malachi 1:8 implies that someone other than Nehemiah was in office, so it may be best to place Malachi just after 433 BC, the year Nehemiah had returned to Persia.

written.label: in the 60s
written.heading: Date and Provenance
written.quote: Irenaeus indicated that Matthew wrote this Gospel while Peter and Paul were in Rome. This would make the time of writing in the 60s.

written.label: before the destruction of Jerusalem (AD 70)
written.heading: Date and Provenance
written.quote: Whether it preceded or followed Mark, most scholars are certain that it was written before the destruction of Jerusalem (AD 70) because the temple is spoken of as still standing (Mt 24:15).

written.label: between AD 60 and 68
written.quote: Second book of the NT, probably written by John Mark of Jerusalem sometime between AD 60 and 68.

written.label: in the 60s
written.heading: Author, Date, Provenance
written.quote: An impressive majority of scholars date Mark in the 60s, with conservatives usually preferring the early years of the decade.

written.label: shortly after AD 70
written.heading: Author, Date, Provenance
written.quote: A small minority of scholars date Mark shortly after AD 70.

written.label: in the 40s or 50s
written.heading: Author, Date, Provenance
written.quote: Another minority suggest a date in the 40s or 50s on the basis of a papyrus fragment discovered in Qumran called 7Q5.

written.label: on or before AD 64
written.heading: Date, Origin, and Destination
written.quote: In all probability the third Gospel was composed in Rome while Paul awaited trial, on or before AD 64.

written.label: after AD 70
written.heading: Date, Origin, and Destination
written.quote: Some argue for a date after AD 70, but this robs Luke 21:20 of its predictive value.

written.label: prior to the death of Paul (AD 64)
written.heading: Date, Origin, and Destination
written.quote: Others suggest a date prior to the death of Paul (AD 64).

written.label: before AD 70
written.heading: Date, Origin, and Destination
written.quote: None of this enables us to date this Gospel with precision. But the weight of evidence points to an early date (before AD 70).
written.prefersQuote: But the weight of evidence points to an early date (before AD 70).

written.label: the last decade of the first century or early in the second
written.heading: Date, Origin, and Destination
written.quote: It has been usual for conservatives and liberals alike to date this writing in the last decade of the first century or early in the second.

written.label: well into the second century
written.heading: Date, Origin, and Destination
written.quote: Some liberal scholars have put it well into the second century, but this is not common, and it is remarkable that there has been such a considerable measure of agreement.

written.label: the last quarter of the first century
written.heading: Date, Origin, Destination
written.quote: Some scholars date it in the last quarter of the first century.

written.label: around AD 70
written.heading: Date, Origin, Destination
written.quote: Other scholars date Acts around AD 70 or shortly thereafter.

written.label: early 60s
written.heading: Date, Origin, Destination
written.quote: A still earlier date, closer to Paul’s Roman imprisonment (early 60s), has been advocated by a number of scholars.

written.label: around AD 57–58
written.heading: Date, Origin, and Destination
written.quote: Paul’s visit to Jerusalem is usually dated around AD 57–58. As such, the Epistle to the Romans was written around the same time.

written.label: AD 55
written.heading: Date and Origin
written.quote: Sometime in AD 55, after hearing reports from Chloe’s household (1 Cor 1:11), who were probably members of Chloe’s house church, he dictated a second letter to Corinth, our 1 Corinthians.

written.heading: Events from AD 50 to 70
written.quote: Then, on his way to Corinth in 56, he wrote 2 Corinthians from Macedonia.

written.label: c. AD 56
written.heading: Destination and Date
written.quote: Under the North Galatian Theory, it is claimed that the letter was written after the events mentioned in Acts 18:23—that is, during the course of the third missionary journey (c. AD 56), possibly while Paul was at Ephesus or soon after.

written.label: pre–AD 50
written.heading: Destination and Date
written.quote: According to this view, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians may be the earliest of his letters (pre–AD 50).

written.label: between AD 59 and 63
written.heading: Date and Origin
written.quote: It is possible that Paul wrote some letters at that time, but most scholars think that Ephesians (along with Colossians, Philemon, and probably Philippians) was written during Paul’s imprisonment at Rome (28:16, 30). This probably took place sometime between AD 59 and 63 and lasted for two years.

written.label: around AD 62
written.heading: Date and Origin
written.quote: The most likely possibility is Rome, in which case the date would be around AD 62.
written.prefersQuote: The traditional location (Rome) seems the most satisfactory, especially when one reflects that Paul was imprisoned there for at least two years (Acts 28:30), and that it took about three weeks to travel from Rome to Philippi.

written.label: c. AD 55
written.heading: Date and Origin
written.quote: So the alternatives of Ephesus (c. AD 55) and Caesarea (c. AD 58) have been proposed.

written.label: c. AD 58
written.heading: Date and Origin
written.quote: So the alternatives of Ephesus (c. AD 55) and Caesarea (c. AD 58) have been proposed.

written.label: AD 60–62
written.heading: Date, Origin, and Destination
written.quote: But the general consensus is that all the Prison Epistles were written in Rome, thus leading to AD 60–62 as the date of Colossians.

written.label: between AD 52 and 55
written.heading: Date, Origin, and Destination
written.quote: Consequently, an increasing number of scholars name that city as the probable place where Paul wrote the prison letters. If that is correct, Paul wrote Colossians sometime between AD 52 and 55.

written.label: early in the year 50
written.heading: Date, Origin, and Destination
written.quote: Since his work in Corinth can be approximately dated, this epistle was probably written early in the year 50, in all likelihood about a year after the first preaching of the gospel in Thessalonica.

written.label: a short time after writing 1 Thessalonians
written.why: The 1 names the letter 1 Thessalonians; it is not a date.
written.heading: Date, Origin, and Destination
written.quote: This indicates that probably a short time after writing 1 Thessalonians, Paul heard of further problems being faced by the Christians in Thessalonica, and in his concern for them, he wrote this second letter.

written.label: much later than 1 Thessalonians
written.why: The 1 names the letter 1 Thessalonians; it is not a date.
written.heading: Date, Origin, and Destination
written.quote: It was written much later than 1 Thessalonians. This is improbable because both Silas and Timothy were still with Paul.

written.label: earlier than 1 Thessalonians
written.why: The 1 names the letter 1 Thessalonians; it is not a date.
written.heading: Date, Origin, and Destination
written.quote: It was written earlier than 1 Thessalonians. In 2:15, however, there is a reference to a letter written previously to Thessalonica, and the early church from the second century certainly called this 2 Thessalonians.

written.label: from 62 to 64
written.heading: Events from AD 50 to 70
written.quote: If so, and if Eusebius was right, then Paul may have spent the two years from 62 to 64 freely ministering back in the eastern provinces. Many conservative scholars date Paul’s First Letter to Timothy and his Letter to Titus from that period.

written.who: Those who do not accept Pauline authorship
written.label: in the generation that followed Paul’s death
written.heading: Date
written.quote: Those who do not accept Pauline authorship of Titus, date this letter, like 1 and 2 Timothy, in the generation that followed Paul’s death.

written.label: between AD 64 and 67
written.heading: Place and Date of Writing
written.quote: The letter was written between AD 64 and 67, with some preference being given to the earlier date.

written.who: Those who do not accept Pauline authorship
written.label: in the generation that followed Paul’s death
written.heading: Date
written.quote: Those who do not accept Pauline authorship of Titus, date this letter, like 1 and 2 Timothy, in the generation that followed Paul’s death.

written.label: from 62 to 64
written.heading: Events from AD 50 to 70
written.quote: If so, and if Eusebius was right, then Paul may have spent the two years from 62 to 64 freely ministering back in the eastern provinces. Many conservative scholars date Paul’s First Letter to Timothy and his Letter to Titus from that period.

written.who: Those who do not accept Pauline authorship
written.label: in the generation that followed Paul’s death
written.heading: Date
written.quote: Those who do not accept Pauline authorship of Titus, date this letter, like 1 and 2 Timothy, in the generation that followed Paul’s death.

written.label: between AD 59 and 63
written.heading: Date and Origin
written.quote: It is possible that Paul wrote some letters at that time, but most scholars think that Ephesians (along with Colossians, Philemon, and probably Philippians) was written during Paul’s imprisonment at Rome (28:16, 30). This probably took place sometime between AD 59 and 63 and lasted for two years.

written.heading: Origin
written.quote: It is difficult to ascertain the location of Paul’s imprisonment at the time of writing.

written.heading: Date
written.quote: Lacking firm information as to the author and recipients of the letter, no certainty exists as to the date of the writing.

written.label: prior to AD 70
written.heading: Date
written.quote: Hence, it may be supposed with some degree of certainty that the letter was written prior to AD 70.

written.label: AD 67–70
written.heading: Date
written.quote: If it was written after Paul’s death, that would put it after AD 67, the traditional date of his execution. Thus, Hebrews may have been written in the period AD 67–70.

written.label: AD 45–49
written.heading: Date, Origin, and Destination
written.quote: Thus, James should be dated AD 45–49.

written.label: AD 64 or 65
written.heading: Destination, Origin, Date
written.quote: The date of 1 Peter is probably AD 64 or 65

written.label: before AD 70 (before his last teaching was forgotten) and after AD 60
written.heading: Date, Origin, Destination
written.quote: Tradition tells us that Peter was martyred about AD 64 in Rome. If that is so, this work was probably written in Rome before AD 70 (before his last teaching was forgotten) and after AD 60 (the earliest date when Peter might have known Paul’s letters).

written.label: near the end of the first century
written.heading: The First Letter of John
written.quote: The date for the composition of 1 John is usually placed near the end of the first century. This date is confirmed by the nature of the heresy condemned and by the references to it in Polycarp and Irenaeus. Greater precision in fixing the date is not possible with the evidence available.

written.heading: The Second Letter of John
written.quote: Information concerning date of writing is inadequate to make any decision. The similarity to 1 John suggests a similar era.

written.heading: The Third Letter of John
written.quote: Again, we have insufficient information to establish date or additional setting.

written.label: between AD 60 and 100
written.heading: Date, Origin, and Destination
written.quote: Since the content of the faith is clearly fixed (Jude 1:3) and the recipients have personally heard the apostles (who may have died already, v 17), the date is probably between AD 60 and 100.

written.label: shortly after the reign of Nero (AD 54–68)
written.heading: Date, Origin, Destination
written.quote: Only two dates for Revelation have received serious support. An early date, shortly after the reign of Nero (AD 54–68), is allegedly supported by references in the book to the persecution of Christians, to the Nero redivivus myth (a revived Nero would be the reincarnation of the evil genius of the whole Roman Empire), to the imperial cult (ch 13), and to the temple (ch 11), which was destroyed in AD 70.

written.label: at the close of Domitian’s reign” (AD 81–96)
written.heading: Date, Origin, Destination
written.quote: The alternate date rests primarily on the early witness of Irenaeus, who stated that the apostle John “saw the revelation . . . at the close of Domitian’s reign” (AD 81–96).

corrections.why: Abraham was 100 years old when Isaac was born (Gen 21:5); Gen 26:5 does not give his age.
